title: Heart and Science: A Story of the Present Time
description: Published in 1883 and Collins's most direct attack on the ethics of experimental science: the story of a vivisectionist who schemes to marry his ward for her money and to use her in his experiments. It is a prose fiction work of 1883 by Wilkie Collins; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Ovid Vere, a gifted young surgeon, falls in love with his orphaned cousin Carmina Graywell; while he travels abroad for his health, his mother, the cold, science-worshipping Mrs Gallilee, persecutes the girl for the sake of her fortune until Carmina collapses into a nervous illness, which the vivisector Dr Benjulia watches as an experiment rather than treat; Ovid returns with a cure learned from a dead doctor's manuscript, and Benjulia, forestalled, sets fire to his laboratory and dies in it, carrying the novel's argument against vivisection.
narrative_structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
principal_characters: Ovid Vere; Carmina Graywell; Mrs Maria Gallilee; Dr Nathan Benjulia; Mr Gallilee; Teresa, Carmina's nurse; Miss Minerva, the governess; Mr Mool, the lawyer
literary_form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1883
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
historical_context: The 1870s-80s, the English anti-vivisection movement and the 1876 Cruelty to Animals Act. The record dates the work as composed in 1883 and first published in 1883 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation novel; social inquiry and the documented survey.
literary_significance: Heart and Science is the central English novel of the anti-vivisection controversy and one of the earliest fictional treatments of the ethics of scientific experiment.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Wilkie Collins. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1883, as novel, by Wilkie Collins. Composed in 1883. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Frozen Deep
description: Written with Charles Dickens in 1856 and performed at Tavistock House in January 1857 with Dickens as Richard Wardour: a melodrama of Arctic exploration, self-sacrifice and the discovery of a rival's worth.
plot_or_argument: Two explorers, Richard Wardour and Frank Aldersley, are rivals for the same woman; in the Arctic, Wardour discovers that the man he is about to kill is his rival and instead carries him across the ice to safety, dying in the effort.
narrative_structure: The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts, each closing on a discovery or a suspense, with the revelation scene placed at the crisis.
principal_characters: Richard Wardour; Frank Aldersley; Clara Burnham; Lucy Crayford; Lieutenant Crayford; Nurse Esther
literary_form: Melodrama in three acts (with Charles Dickens)
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose of the domestic stage: the dialogue of the drawing room and the household, the revelation scene, the timed entrance, and the act ending on a discovery or a suspense. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements.
historical_context: The 1850s, the Franklin expedition and the Arctic searches, and the amateur theatricals of the Dickens circle. The record dates the work as composed in 1856 and first published in 1856 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot, it is catalogued under sensation drama and the domestic stage; imperial adventure romance.
literary_significance: The Frozen Deep is the most famous collaboration of Dickens and Collins, and it shaped the climax of A Tale of Two Cities; it is a key document in the theatrical culture of the 1850s.
attribution_notes: The work is recorded as a joint undertaking with Charles Dickens, the contribution of each being stated in the work-author relationship. Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as William Wilkie Collins. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1856, as melodrama in three acts (with charles dickens), by Wilkie Collins. Composed in 1856. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Modern Love
description: Published in 1862 and the record of the breakdown of the poet's marriage: fifty sixteen-line poems that narrate, in the third person, a husband's discovery of his wife's infidelity and the slow death of their marriage.
plot_or_argument: The sequence follows a husband and wife through the night of the wife's confession, the husband's attempt at generosity, the wife's suicide and the husband's grief; the poems are spoken by a narrator who is neither the husband nor entirely outside him.
narrative_structure: A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
literary_form: Sonnet sequence of fifty sixteen-line poems
meter_and_prosody: Fifty sixteen-line sonnets (four quatrains and a couplet), rhymed abba cddc effe gg, with considerable freedom of stress.
historical_context: The 1861 death of Mary Ellen Meredith, the legal position of a wife under coverture, and the divorce law of 1857. The record dates the work as composed in 1861 and first published in 1862 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet; pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence.
literary_significance: Modern Love is the first English sonnet sequence to treat a marriage from inside and to make the wife's infidelity the subject; it broke the Petrarchan convention of the sequence as idealising worship and made the form available for psychological narrative.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1862, as sonnet sequence of fifty sixteen-line poems, by George Meredith. Composed in 1861. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Ordeal of Richard Feverel: A History of Father and Son
alternative_titles: Ordeal of Richard Feverel: A History of Father and Son
description: Published in 1859 and Meredith's first major novel: the story of a father's 'system' of education and the destruction of his son's happiness by the very theory designed to protect it. It is a prose fiction work of 1859 by George Meredith; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Sir Austin Feverel brings up his son Richard on a rational 'system' that excludes women and feeling; Richard falls in love with Lucy Desborough, marries her secretly, is separated from her by his father's refusal, is deceived into believing her dead, and the novel ends with her death and Richard's own.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
principal_characters: Richard Feverel; Sir Austin Feverel; Lucy Desborough; Austin Wentworth; Adrian Harley; Lady Blandish; Ripton Thompson
literary_form: Novel in three volumes; novel of development
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is epigram, aphorism and the extended metaphor.
historical_context: The 1850s, the Victorian debate on education, the marriage law, and the German and French fiction of education. The record dates the work as composed between 1858 and 1859 and first published in 1859 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot; Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story.
literary_significance: The Ordeal of Richard Feverel is the first English novel of education to make the father's system the villain: its critique of rationalist child-rearing anticipates Butler's and the twentieth-century novel of the family.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1859, as novel in three volumes, by George Meredith. Composed between 1858 and 1859. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Egoist: A Comedy in Narrative
description: Published in 1879 and generally regarded as Meredith's masterpiece: the comedy of Sir Willoughby Patterne, a baronet of perfect self-satisfaction whose engagement to Clara Middleton is gradually destroyed by the revelation of his egoism.
plot_or_argument: Sir Willoughby, having been jilted by Constantia Durham, is engaged to the young and intelligent Clara Middleton, who comes to see that his generosity, his taste and his charm are all functions of his self-love. Her escape is engineered by Vernon Whitford, whom she marries, while Willoughby marries the adoring Laetitia Dale.
narrative_structure: Single-location comedy of manners with a chorus of house guests and a narrator who comments as the 'comic spirit'.
principal_characters: Sir Willoughby Patterne; Clara Middleton; Vernon Whitford; Laetitia Dale; Constantia Durham; Dr Middleton; Mrs Mountstuart Jenkinson; Crossjay Patterne; Horace De Craye
literary_form: Novel in three volumes; realist novel of common life
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is epigram, aphorism and the extended metaphor.
historical_context: The 1870s, the position of the educated woman and the marriage market, the English country house, and the Victorian debate on egoism and altruism. The record dates the work as composed between 1878 and 1879 and first published in 1879 and the corpus places it within Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot; Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: The Egoist is the great English comedy of the ego: its analysis of a self-love that mistakes itself for generosity is a permanent contribution to the psychology of the English gentleman, and its portrait of Clara Middleton is one of the finest studies of a woman's intellectual coming-to-consciousness in the century.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1879, as novel in three volumes, by George Meredith. Composed between 1878 and 1879. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Beauchamp's Career
description: Published in 1875-76 and the most political of Meredith's novels: the story of Nevil Beauchamp, a Radical naval officer who stands for Parliament and is destroyed by his own honesty. It is a prose fiction work of 1876 by George Meredith; it belongs to Sensation Fiction and the Serial Plot and it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Beauchamp campaigns for the Radical cause in a Tory constituency, is rejected by the aristocratic Cecilia Halkett, is drawn back to Renée de Croisnel, the Frenchwoman he loved in his youth, now unhappily married to an old marquis, and, after Cecilia marries the Tory Blackburn Tuckham, marries Jenny Denham, ward of the old Radical Dr Shrapnel, only to drown saving a poor boy from the water; the novel's argument is that his integrity is both his glory and his ruin.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
principal_characters: Nevil Beauchamp; Cecilia Halkett; Renée de Croisnel; Jenny Denham; Dr Shrapnel; Everard Romfrey; Rosamund Culling; Colonel Halkett; Blackburn Tuckham

The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is epigram, aphorism and the extended metaphor.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1876, as novel in three volumes, by George Meredith. Composed between 1874 and 1876. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Diana of the Crossways
description: Published in 1885 and modelled on the life of Caroline Norton: the story of Diana Warwick, a brilliant Irishwoman trapped in a loveless marriage, whose social ruin and financial self-making made the novel a founding text of the New Woman debate.
plot_or_argument: Diana Merion marries the cold Augustus Warwick in haste, partly to escape the advances of her friend Emma's husband, Sir Lukin Dunstane; separated from him after his divorce action fails, she supports herself by writing novels, falls in love with the rising politician Percy Dacier, and, in need of money, sells to the editor Tonans the cabinet secret Dacier has confided to her, which loses her Dacier. After Warwick's death she finally accepts the love of Thomas Redworth.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
principal_characters: Diana Merion (Mrs Warwick); Augustus Warwick; Percy Dacier; Thomas Redworth; Lady Emma Dunstane; Sir Lukin Dunstane; Lord Dannisburgh; Arthur Rhodes; Mr Tonans, the editor
literary_form: Novel in three volumes; new woman
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is epigram, aphorism and the extended metaphor.
historical_context: The 1880s, the Married Women's Property Act of 1882, the position of the separated woman, the law of libel and the political press. The record dates the work as composed between 1884 and 1885 and first published in 1885 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under new woman and marriage-question novel; realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: Diana of the Crossways is the most important English novel of the 1880s on the position of the separated woman and the earning of a living by writing; its heroine is a self-made professional and a central text of late-Victorian feminism.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1885, as novel in three volumes, by George Meredith. Composed between 1884 and 1885. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Shaving of Shagpat: An Arabian Entertainment
alternative_titles: Shaving of Shagpat: An Arabian Entertainment
description: Published in 1855 (dated 1856) and praised by George Eliot and the Pre-Raphaelites: an Arabian romance in the manner of the Thousand and One Nights, in which the barber Shibli Bagarag must shave the miraculous hair of the tyrant Shagpat.
plot_or_argument: Shibli Bagarag, a barber of the Persian city, is enlisted by the enchantress Noorna bin Noorka to shave the single hair on the head of the tyrant Shagpat, which makes him invulnerable; the quest takes him through a series of magic kingdoms, and the tale ends with the tyrant's fall and the release of his people.
narrative_structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
principal_characters: Shibli Bagarag; Noorna bin Noorka; Shagpat; Baba Mustapha, his uncle; Karaz, the genie; Rabesqurat; Goorelka
literary_form: Oriental romance (prose fantasy)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The author's characteristic manner is epigram, aphorism and the extended metaphor.
historical_context: The 1850s, the Victorian taste for the Oriental tale (Lane's Thousand and One Nights, 1838-40). The record dates the work as composed in 1855 and first published in 1856 and it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.
literary_significance: The Shaving of Shagpat is the finest English Oriental prose romance of the century and the work in which Meredith's comic and allegorical gifts first appeared.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1856, as oriental romance (prose fantasy), by George Meredith. Composed in 1855. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Far from the Madding Crowd
alternative_titles: Far from the Madding Crowd: A Pastoral Romance
description: Serialised anonymously in the Cornhill Magazine in 1874 and published in two volumes: the novel that made Hardy famous and the first of the Wessex novels to be set in the fully realised rural world of his invention.
plot_or_argument: Bathsheba Everdene inherits a farm at Weatherbury and is courted by the shepherd Gabriel Oak, the prosperous farmer William Boldwood and the soldier Frank Troy; she marries Troy, who is killed by Boldwood, and after years of widowhood and the ruin of Boldwood she marries Oak.
narrative_structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
principal_characters: Bathsheba Everdene; Gabriel Oak; William Boldwood; Frank Troy; Fanny Robin; Joseph Poorgrass; Jan Coggan; Liddy Smallbury
literary_form: Novel (Cornhill Magazine, 1874)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs.
historical_context: The 1870s, the agricultural depression and the decline of the yeoman farmer, the corn market and the harvest. The record dates the work as composed between 1872 and 1874 and first published in 1874 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School; Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
literary_significance: Far from the Madding Crowd established the Wessex novel and made Hardy a major novelist; its integration of rural labour, landscape and the marriage plot is the model for the English regional novel.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised anonymously in The Cornhill Magazine from January to December 1874 and published in two volumes by Smith, Elder in November 1874. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Return of the Native
description: Published in 1878 and the most tragic of the early Wessex novels: the story of Eustacia Vye, the passionate and thwarted woman of Egdon Heath, and of her marriage to Clym Yeobright, the native who returns from Paris to teach.
plot_or_argument: Eustacia Vye, longing to escape Egdon, marries Clym Yeobright, who has returned from the diamond trade to become a schoolmaster; his blindness, the interference of his mother, and Eustacia's rekindled attachment to Damon Wildeve lead to her flight and the drowning of Eustacia and Wildeve in the weir.
narrative_structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
principal_characters: Eustacia Vye; Clym Yeobright; Damon Wildeve; Thomasin Yeobright; Diggory Venn; Mrs Yeobright; Captain Vye; Susan Nunsuch
literary_form: Novel (Belgravia, 1878); realist novel of common life
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs.
historical_context: The 1840s-70s, the heath economy of furze-cutting, the return of the colonial emigrant, and the Victorian debate on education and the 'native' who returns. The record dates the work as composed in 1878 and first published in 1878 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
literary_significance: The Return of the Native is the great English novel of the heath and of the woman who is destroyed by place; its opening description of Egdon is one of the most famous in English fiction and its fatalism is the purest statement of Hardy's philosophy before Tess.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised in Belgravia from January to December 1878 and published in three volumes by Smith, Elder in November 1878. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Mayor of Casterbridge: The Life and Death of a Man of Character
description: Published in 1886 and generally regarded as the most perfectly constructed of Hardy's novels: the story of Michael Henchard, who sells his wife and daughter at a fair in a drunken impulse and lives to be destroyed by the return of his own past.
plot_or_argument: Henchard sells his wife Susan and baby Elizabeth-Jane at Weydon-Priors fair, swears an oath of temperance for twenty-one years, and becomes mayor of Casterbridge; Susan returns, Henchard's rival Donald Farfrae rises in the town, the wife sale is discovered, and Henchard's fortune, reputation and relationships are progressively destroyed, ending in his death alone in a hut on Egdon Heath.
narrative_structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
principal_characters: Michael Henchard; Susan Henchard; Elizabeth-Jane Newson; Donald Farfrae; Lucetta Le Sueur; Joshua Jopp; Abel Whittle; Richard Newson
literary_form: Novel (Graphic, 1886); realist novel of common life
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs.
historical_context: The 1840s, the corn trade and the agricultural depression, the town of Dorchester, and the Victorian debate on character and determinism. The record dates the work as composed between 1884 and 1886 and first published in 1886 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; sensation novel.
literary_significance: The Mayor of Casterbridge is the classic English novel of character and fate: its wife-sale opening is one of the most famous scenes in English fiction, and its study of a man destroyed by his own past is the purest statement of Hardy's tragic method.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised in The Graphic from January to October 1886 and published in three volumes by Osgood, McIlvaine in May 1886 with the subtitle The Life and Death of a Man of Character. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Tess of the d'Urbervilles: A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented
description: Published in 1891 with the subtitle 'A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented' and the most controversial of Hardy's novels: the story of Tess Durbeyfield, seduced by Alec d'Urberville, married and abandoned by Angel Clare, and destroyed by the double standard of her society.
plot_or_argument: Tess Durbeyfield, whose family believes itself descended from the Norman d'Urbervilles, is sent to claim kin and is seduced by Alec; she bears a child who dies, works at the dairy at Talbothays, marries Angel Clare, confesses her past on the wedding night, is abandoned by him, is driven back to Alec, and when Angel returns she kills Alec and is arrested at Stonehenge and executed at Wintoncester.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
principal_characters: Tess Durbeyfield; Alec d'Urberville; Angel Clare; Joan Durbeyfield; John Durbeyfield; Marian; Retty Priddle; Izz Huett; Liza-Lu; Sorrow
literary_form: Novel (Graphic, 1891; three volumes 1891)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs.
historical_context: The 1880s-90s, the decline of the rural labourer, the evangelical revival, the Victorian sexual double standard, and the publication history of the novel. The record dates the work as composed between 1889 and 1891 and first published in 1891 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy; Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; naturalist and determinist novel.
literary_significance: Tess is the central English novel of the sexual double standard and one of the great novels of the nineteenth century: its defence of Tess as 'a pure woman' made it the founding text of the novel of social justice for women and a permanent point of reference for feminist criticism.
attribution_notes: First published in a censored serial version in the Graphic (1891) and then in three volumes with the full text restored; the standard text is the Wessex Edition of 1912.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised in bowdlerised form in The Graphic from July to December 1891 and published in three volumes by Osgood, McIlvaine in November 1891 with the full title Tess of the d'Urbervilles: A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented. The research status is partial. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Jude the Obscure
alternative_titles: Jude the Obscure: A Straightforward Novel
description: Published in 1895 and Hardy's last novel: the story of Jude Fawley, a stonemason refused admission to Christminster university, and of his cousin Sue Bridehead, whose intellectual freedom and sexual fear make her one of the most complex women in Victorian fiction.
plot_or_argument: Jude Fawley studies the classics in a village and is tricked into marriage with Arabella Donn; he goes to Christminster, meets Sue Bridehead, and lives with her unmarried after she leaves her husband Phillotson; their children are killed in a murder-suicide that Jude interprets as a judgement, Sue returns to Phillotson in penance, and Jude dies in the rain at the Remembrance Day celebrations.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end.
principal_characters: Jude Fawley; Sue Bridehead; Arabella Donn; Richard Phillotson; Little Father Time; Mrs Edlin; Uncle Drusilla Fawley
literary_form: Novel (Harper's, 1894-95; one volume 1895)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of naturalism: the clinical accumulation of physiological and economic detail, the flat unjudging sentence, the dialect transcribed at length, and the plot driven by heredity, appetite and environment rather than by choice. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs.
historical_context: The 1890s, the university question and the exclusion of the working class, the marriage law, the 'New Woman' debate, and the publication crisis that followed the novel's reception. The record dates the work as composed between 1892 and 1895 and first published in 1895 and the corpus places it within American Naturalism and the Determinist Tragedy; The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under naturalist and determinist novel; realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: Jude the Obscure is the most radical of the Victorian novels on class, education and marriage, and the novel whose reception ended Hardy's career as a novelist. Its critique of the university made it a founding text of the literature of class exclusion, and it stands at the exact boundary between Victorian and modern fiction.
attribution_notes: The serial in Harper's Monthly (1894-95) was heavily cut; the 1895 one-volume edition restored the text and provoked the attack that led Hardy to abandon fiction.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Osgood, McIlvaine in November 1895, dated 1896, after serialisation in Harper's New Monthly Magazine from December 1894; the book was burnt publicly at Wakefield in 1896. The research status is partial. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Dynasts: An Epic-Drama of the War with Napoleon
alternative_titles: Dynasts: An Epic-Drama of the War with Napoleon
description: Published in three parts between 1903 and 1908 and the most ambitious English verse drama of the modern period: an epic of the Napoleonic wars, from Trafalgar to Waterloo, with the 'Phantom Intelligences' of the Immanent Will commenting on the action.
plot_or_argument: The drama follows the campaigns of 1805-1815 across Europe, with Napoleon, Wellington, Nelson, Pitt and the common soldiers of Wessex as its figures; the Spirits watch from above, and the work ends with the retreat from Moscow and the field of Waterloo.
narrative_structure: A play in acts in blank verse, with the lyrical interludes and choruses set in shorter lines and in rhyme.
principal_characters: Napoleon Bonaparte; Wellington; Nelson; Pitt; the Spirit of the Years; the Spirit of the Pities; the Spirit Ironic; the Spirit Sinister
literary_form: Epic-drama in three parts, nineteen acts and 130 scenes
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse for the principal speeches and lyric metres for the choruses, with prose for the domestic scenes.
historical_context: The 1890s-1900s, the new imperialism and the Boer War, and the Edwardian taste for the pageant and the historical spectacle. The record dates the work as composed between 1897 and 1908 and first published in 1903 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice, it is catalogued under victorian verse drama and revived tragedy; war narrative of the common soldier.
literary_significance: The Dynasts is the greatest English verse drama of the twentieth century's beginning and the fullest statement of Hardy's philosophy of the Immanent Will; it is the last English epic.

title: Wessex Poems and Other Verses
description: Published in 1898, Hardy's first collection of verse after thirty years of novel-writing, with his own illustrations: poems of Wessex landscape, of the dead, of the Napoleonic wars and of the ironies of circumstance.
plot_or_argument: The collection ranges from the ballad-like 'The Dance at the Phoenix' and the Napoleonic 'The Sergeant's Song' to the elegiac 'Friends Beyond' and the sardonic 'Nature's Questioning'.
narrative_structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
literary_form: Poetry collection (with the author's own drawings)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs.
historical_context: The 1890s, Hardy's return to the poetry he had written since the 1860s, and the decline of the rural community. The record dates the work as composed between 1860 and 1896 and first published in 1898 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
literary_significance: Wessex Poems began Hardy's career as a major poet and set the tone of his verse; it is the volume from which the twentieth-century revival of Hardy's poetry dates.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1898, as poetry collection (with the author's own drawings), by Thomas Hardy. Composed between 1860 and 1896. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Satires of Circumstance, Lyrics and Reveries
description: Published in November 1914 and the volume that contains the 'Poems of 1912-13', the greatest English sequence of mourning after In Memoriam: the poems written after Hardy's visit to Cornwall and to Emma's birthplace following her death in 1912.
plot_or_argument: The 'Poems of 1912-13' revisit the places of the early marriage — St Juliot, Boscastle, Beeny Cliff, Pendennis — and record the speaker's grief, guilt and belated recognition of the wife he had neglected; the volume also contains the 'Satires of Circumstance' and the lyrics of the Wessex world.
narrative_structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.
literary_form: Poetry collection; pastoral elegy
meter_and_prosody: Verse. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs.
historical_context: The death of Emma Hardy in November 1912, the visit to Cornwall in March 1913, and the Edwardian and Georgian poetry of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1912 and 1914 and first published in 1914 and it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; idyll and domestic narrative poem.
literary_significance: The 'Poems of 1912-13' are the central English elegies of the twentieth century; their honesty about a failed marriage made them the model for the modern confessional elegy and established Hardy as a major poet.

title: The Woodlanders
description: Published in 1887 and Hardy's own favourite among his novels: the story of the woodland economy of Little Hintock and of Grace Melbury, educated above her neighbours and returned to marry the woodlander Giles Winterborne.
plot_or_argument: Grace Melbury, the timber merchant's daughter, is educated and returns engaged to Giles Winterborne; she marries the doctor Edred Fitzpiers instead, is betrayed by his affair with Mrs Charmond, and after Giles's death in a storm and Fitzpiers's reform she returns to her husband.
narrative_structure: A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly.
principal_characters: Grace Melbury; Giles Winterborne; Edred Fitzpiers; Felice Charmond; George Melbury; Marty South; Suke Damson; Tim Tangs; Grammer Oliver; John South
literary_form: Novel (Macmillan's Magazine, 1886-87)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The author's characteristic manner is regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs.
historical_context: The 1880s, the decline of the woodland trades and the coming of the railway, and the position of the educated woman in a rural community. The record dates the work as composed between 1885 and 1887 and first published in 1887 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; local-colour sketch and the regional portrait.
literary_significance: The Woodlanders is the finest English novel of the woodland economy: its treatment of the destruction of a rural trade by the market and the railway is a key text for the ecological criticism of Victorian fiction.

bibliographical_notes: Published in three volumes by Macmillan in March 1887, after serialisation in Macmillan's Magazine from May 1886. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Treasure Island
alternative_titles: Treasure Island; or, The Mutiny of the Hispaniola
description: Serialised as The Sea-Cook in Young Folks in 1881-82 and published in 1883: the founding modern adventure novel, and the book that fixed the image of the treasure map, the one-legged pirate and the boy hero for all later fiction.
plot_or_argument: Jim Hawkins finds a treasure map in the sea chest of the dead Billy Bones, sails on the Hispaniola with Squire Trelawney and Dr Livesey, discovers that the crew has been recruited by the mutineer Long John Silver, survives the mutiny and the island, and returns with the treasure.
narrative_structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.

meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of adventure: the first-person or closely focalised narrative of pursuit and escape, the set-piece chapter, the exact vocabulary of weapons, ships, terrain and travel, and the rapid unreflective sentence. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is classical purity and economy of prose.

The record dates the work as composed between 1881 and 1883 and first published in 1883 and the corpus places it within Muscular Christianity and the Schoolboy Tale of Empire, it is catalogued under imperial adventure romance; children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.

title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
description: Published in January 1886 and written in a few weeks after a dream: the story of a London physician who separates the good and evil elements of his nature by a drug, and of the double who takes his place.
plot_or_argument: Mr Utterson, a lawyer, investigates the strange relationship between his friend Dr Henry Jekyll and the violent Edward Hyde; Hyde murders Sir Danvers Carew, Jekyll withdraws, and the final confession explains that Jekyll's potion allowed him to become Hyde at will, until the transformations became involuntary and Hyde took over.
narrative_structure: Three narrators: Utterson's third-person narrative, Lanyon's statement, and Jekyll's full statement of the case.
principal_characters: Henry Jekyll; Edward Hyde; Gabriel John Utterson; Richard Enfield; Dr Hastie Lanyon; Sir Danvers Carew; Mr Poole
literary_form: Novella (published 9 January 1886; 'shilling shocker')
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The author's characteristic manner is classical purity and economy of prose.
historical_context: The 1880s, the new psychology of the divided self, the Darwinian account of the beast within, and the Edinburgh of Deacon Brodie. The record dates the work as composed between 1885 and 1886 and first published in 1886 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under ghost story and scientific supernatural tale; naturalist and determinist novel.
literary_significance: Jekyll and Hyde is the central English myth of the divided self: it gave the language the terms for dual personality and addiction, and it stands at the origin of both the modern psychological novel and the horror genre.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as R. L. S. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1886, as novella (published 9 january 1886; 'shilling shocker'), by Robert Louis Stevenson. Composed between 1885 and 1886. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Kidnapped: Being Memoirs of the Adventures of David Balfour in the Year 1751
description: Published in 1886 and set in the Highlands after the Jacobite rising of 1745: the story of David Balfour, cheated of his inheritance, kidnapped, shipwrecked, and thrown into the company of the Jacobite swordsman Alan Breck Stewart.
plot_or_argument: David Balfour is kidnapped on his uncle's orders, shipwrecked off Mull, joins Alan Breck in the escape from the brig Covenant, is accused of the murder of the Red Fox at Appin, and flees with Alan across the Highlands to Edinburgh, where he recovers his estate.
narrative_structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
principal_characters: David Balfour; Alan Breck Stewart; Ebenezer Balfour; Colin Campbell (the Red Fox); James of the Glens; Captain Hoseason; Cluny Macpherson

title: The Master of Ballantrae: A Winter's Tale
description: Published in 1889 and the darkest of Stevenson's romances: the story of the two Durie brothers of the 1745 rising, the one who goes out and the one who stays, and of the hatred that survives across the world.
plot_or_argument: James Durie, the Master of Ballantrae, joins the Jacobites while his brother Henry stays at home and marries the woman they both love; James returns from India and France to torment Henry, and the brothers travel to America, where they die in the North Woods, James's body guarded by Henry until both are found.
narrative_structure: A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close.
principal_characters: James Durie; Henry Durie; Alison Graeme; Ephraim Mackellar; Mr Henry's factor; Secundra Dass; Lord Durrisdeer; Miss Katharine

title: A Child's Garden of Verses
description: Published in 1885 and the most influential English children's poetry collection of the century: sixty-four poems of childhood, illness, imagination and the country house, written from the memory of Stevenson's own sickly Edinburgh childhood.
plot_or_argument: The poems move from 'The Land of Counterpane' and the sickroom to the garden, 'The Land of Nod', 'My Shadow', the 'Swing' and 'Foreign Lands', and end with the child's view of the adult world in 'The Unseen Playmate' and 'Happy Thought'.
narrative_structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
literary_form: Poetry collection for children
meter_and_prosody: Mostly four-line stanzas in iambic tetrameter or trimeter, with a few longer lyrical forms.
historical_context: The 1880s, the Victorian invention of childhood as a separate imaginative world, and the Stevenson family's Edinburgh houses. title: The Black Arrow: A Tale of the Two Roses
description: Published in 1888 though serialised in 1883: a romance of the Wars of the Roses in which Dick Shelton, a young Lancastrian, takes to the greenwood to avenge his father and win the heiress Joanna Sedley.

title: The Ebb-Tide: A Trio and Quartette
description: Published in 1894 and the grimmest of Stevenson's Pacific works: three beachcombers in Papeete take command of a plague ship carrying champagne, and the story of what they find on the island they sail to.
plot_or_argument: Herrick, Davis and Huish, destitute in Tahiti, take the schooner Farallone whose crew has died of smallpox and whose cargo is champagne; they reach an island occupied by the missionary Attwater, who holds them in his power, and the novel ends with Huish's death and Herrick's moral awakening.
narrative_structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel of pursuit and escape in chapters, each carrying a set piece of travel, combat or discovery.
principal_characters: Robert Herrick; Captain John Davis; Huish, the Cockney clerk; William John Attwater
literary_form: Novel (with Lloyd Osbourne; serialised in To-day, 1893)

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
description: Published in Lippincott's Monthly Magazine in June 1890 and expanded for book form in 1891: the story of a beautiful young man whose portrait ages and corrupts while he remains untouched, and the central English novel of aestheticism.
plot_or_argument: Lord Henry Wotton persuades Dorian Gray that youth and beauty are the only things worth having; Dorian wishes that the portrait painted by Basil Hallward would age instead of him, and the wish is granted. He lives a life of concealed vice, murders Basil, blackmails Alan Campbell, and finally stabs the portrait, which restores him to his ruined age and kills him.
narrative_structure: Third-person narrative with interpolated chapters of aphorism and a chapter of Dorian's collection of corrupting books.
principal_characters: Dorian Gray; Lord Henry Wotton; Basil Hallward; Sibyl Vane; James Vane; Alan Campbell; Lady Agatha; Lord Fermor
literary_form: Novel (Lippincott's Monthly Magazine, 1890; expanded 1891)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is the inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram.
